claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Quantitative descriptors derived from high-resolution imaging and chemical mapping can represent the length scales and volume fractions of chemical-fluctuation domains.
A transfer-learning model pre-trained on related alloy systems can be calibrated using a limited set of HfNbTiVAl10 tensile and fracture tests.
The proposed microstructural descriptors capture the multiscale chemical fluctuations in the hierarchical structure.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations mediate local stress distributions.
Local stress distributions control the alloy's elastic, plastic, and fracture responses.
Embedding physically relevant microstructural information in a transfer-learning model enables knowledge from related alloys to be used to predict the effects of local heterogeneity.

The proposed framework will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness more accurately than conventional calculation methods and standard machine-learning models lacking explicit microstructural descriptors.
The proposed framework will reduce computational overhead relative to high-fidelity first-principles and CALPHAD calculations.
The proposed method is expected to decrease prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by 20–30%.
The proposed method is expected to reduce computational time by 50–70% relative to the baseline methods.
The model will lose reliability when processing changes or alloy modifications generate microstructural features outside its calibrated descriptor space.
The model will lose reliability when imaging or chemical mapping does not resolve the microstructural detail required by its descriptors.
Prediction gains depend on the representativeness and quality of the calibration data.
Prediction gains depend on the fidelity of the microstructural descriptors.
A blinded prospective benchmark will treat failure to obtain both a statistically significant accuracy improvement of at least 10% and a computational-time reduction of at least 20% as falsification.
